about: The look & feel board's history, one step per request. Each step lists the board items it added or changed, as they read at the end of that step. mockups/history_log.py turns this into HISTORY.html; `python3 history_log.py --record <step-id>` appends the changes since the last step from board/items.json.

steps.title: The look & feel board
steps.asked: Set up a digital whiteboard as an HTML page, with text, images and video, to sketch out how the game should look and feel before planning the assets and the build.
changed: A private board page on claude.ai that saves everything to its own database
Nine sections, from Overall vibe to Sound & music, each with a note of starter questions
Notes, images, video, links and color swatches, each of which can be marked Want, Maybe or Avoid
A section in CLAUDE.md with the board's link

items.text:
# How to use this board
- Add notes, images, video clips, links and color swatches with the buttons up top, or drop and paste them anywhere
- Mark anything **Want**, **Maybe** or **Avoid** so we agree on what fits and what doesn't
- Each section has starter questions. Answer them, edit them, delete them, or add sections of your own
- I read this board before we plan, so the more that's here, the closer the game gets to what you picture
items.author: claude

items.text:
# What should it feel like?
- Three words for the mood of the game
- Grim and oppressive, bright and heroic, or something else?
- Which games, films, books or art capture the feeling?
- What should a player say after their first hour?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# How should it look?
- 2D or 3D? Pixel art, hand-painted, low-poly, stylized or realistic?
- Drop in images of the style you want, and mark the ones to avoid
- Add color swatches to sketch the palette
items.author: claude

items.text:
# How do we see the world?
- Isometric, top-down or an angled third-person view?
- How close is the camera? How much of the screen is the hero?
- Fixed angle, or can the player rotate it?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# How should a fight feel?
- Fast and twitchy, or slow and heavy?
- Hordes of weak enemies, or a few tough ones?
- How loud is a hit: screen shake, hit-stop, gore, big damage numbers?
- Clips of combat you love are perfect here
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Who is in it?
- The player: one fixed hero, classes, or build your own?
- What are the enemies: monsters, people, machines, something stranger?
- Bosses: how big and how dramatic?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Where does it take place?
- Setting: dark fantasy, sci-fi, myth, something else?
- Hand-built levels, randomly generated dungeons, or a mix?
- Places you can already picture: caves, cities, ruins, forests?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# What do you collect and grow?
- How much loot drops: a shower or a trickle?
- Skill trees, gear, crafting: which matters most?
- How long should a full playthrough take?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# What is on screen?
- Health and resource bars, a skill bar, a minimap?
- Minimal and clean, or ornate and themed?
- How should the inventory and item tooltips look?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# What does it sound like?
- Music: orchestral, ambient, metal, synth, something else?
- How punchy should hits and spells sound?
- Voice acting, or text only?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Move with WASD
- W, A, S and D move the character
- Holding two keys walks diagonally
- Assumed: directions follow the screen, so W walks up the screen and A walks left
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Aim with the mouse
- The mouse aims, separately from movement
- You can run one way while aiming and attacking another
- This scheme is often called twin-stick controls
items.author: claude

items.caption: Walking toward the bottom-left while aiming up-right. The character keeps facing the cursor.
items.author: claude

items.text:
# What this means for animation
The character can face one way while moving another, so a forward run alone won't do. It needs movement animations for each direction relative to where it faces: forward, backward, and strafing left and right, blended for the diagonals.

That raises the number of animations we have to make, so it's worth settling early.
items.author: claude

items.text:

- Is there a dodge or dash, and on which key?
- Is moving backward slower than moving forward?
- Should a gamepad work too (left stick moves, right stick aims)?

# What this means for animation
- **Not attacking:** a normal forward walk and run are enough, since the character faces where it goes

items.text:
# Camera control
- Hold the **right mouse button** and move the mouse to orbit the camera around the hero, like in WoW
- Sideways turns the view around the hero
- Up and down changes the angle: from straight down, through the default high view, to low behind the hero
items.author: claude

items.text:
# What a free camera changes
- **WASD follows the camera:** W walks away from the camera, whichever way it faces
- **Right click is taken,** so attacks and skills use left click and the keyboard
- **Low angles show the horizon,** so we need a sky, distant forest and haze to hide the edge of the map
- **Trees must fade** between the camera and the hero at every angle
- **Aiming gets touchy at low angles,** where the ground is seen almost edge-on
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Open camera questions
- Zoom in and out with the mouse wheel?
- How low and how high can the camera go?
- When you let go of the right button, does the camera stay where you left it?
- Should it ever swing back behind the hero by itself?
- Does the mouse cursor hide while you rotate?

steps.title: The whole of Act 1
steps.asked: Look at the whole of Act 1: 10–15 quests and 1–2 hours of play, laid out like act1_layout.png. Past the town comes Storskogen (the fairmeadow), a vast forest with open plains, thick forest, raised ground and hollows, all with slopes you can walk. Make top-down blueprints of the act and screenshots from different zones at different camera angles.
changed: The act traced from your sketch at about 1.2 m per unit: seven areas and about 1.2 km² to walk
Storskogen: open meadows, a thicket, an esker ridge, a lookout hill and a kettle-hole hollow, and no slope in the act steeper than 20°
12 quests (7 main, 5 side): about 80 minutes for the story, 1 h 55 min for everything
Two blueprints and ten screenshots, A–J, all made from the same world data

items.text:
# Act 1 at a glance
- Seven areas traced from your act1_layout.png, at about 1.2 m per sketch unit
- **Tallmo** (town) opens onto **Storskogen**, the hub
- From Storskogen: **Härddalen** to the north-east, **Gamla gården** to the east, **Dimskogen** to the north-west
- Dimskogen leads down to **Dimmyren**, then a winding path west to **Ödeskogen**, where the act ends
- About 1.2 km² to walk; Storskogen alone is about 720 × 650 m
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Zone names (suggestions)
- **Tallmo**: the town
- **Storskogen**: the fairmeadow
- **Härddalen**: Hearthvale
- **Gamla gården**: the Old Courtyard
- **Dimskogen**: the Misty Woods
- **Dimmyren**: the Misty Swamp
- **Ödeskogen**: the Forsaken Forest
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Main story (placeholder)
- **1 Vägen ut:** clear the road to the crossroads
- **4 Vårdkasen:** light the beacon on the lookout hill
- **5 Den kalla härden:** find the survivors of the burned farm
- **8 Förvaltarens brev:** the steward's letter points to the fog
- **9 När dimman kommer:** follow the wisps into Dimskogen
- **11 De sjunkna stenarna:** raise the sunken rune stones
- **12 Den hornkrönte:** face the Antlered One at the dead tree

Plus 5 side quests. Main story about 80 min, everything about 1 h 55 min.

items.text:
# Storskogen terrain
- Open meadows: **Stora ängen** and **Hagen**
- Dense pine and spruce: **Tätskogen**
- Raised: **Åsen**, an 11 m esker ridge with a trail on top, and **Utsiktsberget**, an 18 m lookout hill
- Lowered: **Trollgrytan**, a 10 m deep kettle hole with a grove, a tarn and a stone circle
- Steepest slope anywhere in Act 1 is 20°, so all of it is walkable

items.text:
# Open questions
- Do the Swedish zone names work, or should some stay English?
- Should the fog stay with Dimskogen and beyond, or roll in and out anywhere?
- Is Tallmo big enough, or should it grow?
- Is 7 main and 5 side quests the right mix?
- Do the zone sizes feel right for 1–2 hours?

steps.title: Worn paths
steps.asked: Where the gravel path meets the grass there is a hard line between the brown path and the green grass. Make the transition faded and smooth, and give the path more texture so it shows it's actually gravel and pebbles. The paths come from feet wearing down the grass that grew there, so a hard line makes no sense.
changed: The path edge fades out: the grass thins in ragged clumps toward the path, and the grass along it turns dry and trampled
Visible gravel: small flat stones of mixed sizes on packed dirt, densest in the middle, with a few kicked out into the grass
Low grass tufts and pebbles placed along the edges, without moving anything else in the scenes
The needle litter under trees fades out instead of ending in a zigzag
Act 1 roads now show where they cross meadows and the town; the meadow grass used to be painted over them
Before/after pairs from the forest and Act 1, with close-ups at full resolution
found: With the gravel showing, the paths read a little greyer than the old brown band; the mix of dirt and gravel is easy to tune
In Dimskogen the dark floor and the fog hide the path, so that shot barely changes

changed: text
items.text:
# Props and details
- **Rocks:** chunky, with uneven faces of mixed shapes and sizes, not lots of small triangles
- **Tree trunks:** one piece, straight or gently leaning
- **Paths:** winding, uneven width, curved forks, and worn into the grass: no hard edge, the grass thins out toward them, and gravel and pebbles show in the dirt
- **Berries:** grouped in patches, sitting on the bushes
- **Avoid:** blocky purple flower clumps
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Worn paths
Paths are worn into the grass by feet, so they no longer end in a hard line:
- **Edges:** the grass thins out in ragged clumps toward the path, and the grass along it is drier and trampled
- **Gravel:** small flat stones of mixed sizes on packed dirt, densest in the middle, with a few kicked out into the grass
- **Props:** low grass tufts and pebbles along the edges break up the outline
- **Also:** roads now show through meadows and the town, where the meadow grass used to cover them, and the needle litter under trees fades out instead of ending in a zigzag

With the gravel showing, the paths read a little greyer. The mix of dirt and gravel is easy to tune.

steps.title: Tree portfolio
steps.asked: Start a portfolio of assets, beginning with trees to replace the current ones: the trees of a Swedish forest from your new reference sheet, as low-poly 3D models made in Blender with Python and viewable in Blender. Trunks and branches low-poly; leaf clumps made with crossed planes, several copies of a leaf card intersecting at different angles around the same centre.
changed: Scots pine, silver birch, Norway spruce, aspen, rowan, alder and juniper, two variants of each, in assets/trees/tree_portfolio.blend
Faceted low-poly trunks and branches, coloured per face: grey-to-orange pine, white birch with black marks, dark multi-stemmed alder
Leaf clumps of three crossed cards (one lying flat for the view from above), with normals pointing out from the crown so it shades as one volume
A leaf card per species, drawn by script with transparent backgrounds, including rowan with red berries and juniper with blue berries
In the file: two rows with name signs and a person for scale beside each tree, and a mixed grove with a camera at the game's angle
found: The first crowns were far too thin, and the spruce looked like a bare skeleton: the cards had to be much fuller and the clumps bigger
The first pine came out as a lollipop; a wider, flatter crown of separate pads on spreading branches made it read as a Scots pine
Heights are about 70% of real trees, to suit the high game camera; the spruce is heavy at about 1,800 leaf cards

items.text:
# Tree portfolio
The seven trees from your reference sheet, two variants of each, as low-poly models built in Blender by Python scripts:
- **Trunk and branches:** faceted low-poly tubes, coloured per face
- **Leaf clumps:** crossed planes, three copies of a leaf card crossing at their centre, one lying flat for the view from above
- **Shading:** the cards' normals point out from the crown, so it shades as one rounded volume

Open `assets/trees/tree_portfolio.blend` in Blender to look around; it opens on the first row with materials shown.
